stem: Ethane, with the molecular formula C₂H₆ has
solution:
Build the structure and count every shared pair.

\(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_3\)

- **Six C–H bonds** — three hydrogens on each carbon.
- **One C–C bond** joining the two carbons.

\(6 + 1 = 7\), so the answer is **(B)**.

The single C–C bond is the one most often forgotten; counting only the hydrogens gives (A). Each carbon then has four bonds and each hydrogen one, which is the check that the structure is right.
groundedIn: §4.2.1 Saturated and Unsaturated Carbon Compounds, which builds ethane by linking the carbons with a single bond and then satisfying the remaining valencies with hydrogen (Fig. 4.6), and §4.1 for a covalent bond being one shared pair.

stem: Butanone is a four-carbon compound with the functional group
solution:
The **suffix names the functional group**, and butanone ends in **-one**.

From Table 4.4:

- *-oic acid* → carboxylic acid, so (A) would be butanoic acid.
- *-al* → aldehyde, so (B) would be butanal.
- **-one → ketone**, which is butanone. **(C)**
- *-ol* → alcohol, so (D) would be butanol.

Its structure is \(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CO} - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_3\), with the carbonyl group on a carbon **inside** the chain — which is what distinguishes a ketone from an aldehyde.
groundedIn: §4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds with Table 4.4, which lists the suffix for each class of compound and gives propanone as the ketone example.

stem: While cooking, if the bottom of the vessel is getting blackened on the outside, it means that

options.label: A
options.text: the food is not cooked completely

options.label: B
options.text: the fuel is not burning completely

solution:
The blackening is **soot**, which is unburnt carbon, and soot is the signature of **incomplete combustion** — **(B)**.

A stove has air holes so that a sufficiently oxygen-rich mixture burns with a clean blue flame. If those holes get blocked, the supply of air is limited, the fuel burns incompletely with a yellow sooty flame, and the soot deposits on the vessel. The fuel is also being wasted.

- (A) is about the food, not the flame.
- (C) may make a fire hard to light, but the blackening is caused by the air supply.
- (D) is the opposite: complete combustion gives a clean flame and no deposit.
groundedIn: §4.3.1 Combustion with Activities 4.3 and 4.4, which state that limiting the supply of air gives a sooty flame and that blackened vessel bottoms mean the air holes are blocked and fuel is being wasted.

stem: Explain the nature of the covalent bond using the bond formation in CH₃Cl.
solution:
A **covalent bond is formed by the sharing of an electron pair between two atoms**, so that both attain a completely filled outermost shell.

**The atoms involved in \(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}\).**

- **Carbon** has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more for an octet. It can neither gain four (a nucleus of six protons could not hold ten electrons) nor lose four (that would cost far too much energy), so it **shares** instead.
- Each **hydrogen** has 1 electron and needs 1 more to fill its K shell.
- **Chlorine** has 7 valence electrons and needs 1 more for an octet.

**The bonding.** Carbon forms **four single covalent bonds** — one shared pair with each of the three hydrogen atoms, and one shared pair with the chlorine atom:

\(\text{H} - \overset{\displaystyle |}{\underset{\displaystyle |}{\text{C}}} - \text{Cl}\) with the two remaining bonds going to hydrogen atoms

**The result.** Carbon now counts 8 electrons round itself (4 of its own plus 4 shared in), each hydrogen counts 2, and chlorine counts 8. Every atom has a noble-gas configuration, and **no ions are formed** — which is why \(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}\), like other covalent compounds, has a low melting and boiling point and does not conduct electricity.
groundedIn: §4.1 Bonding in Carbon — the Covalent Bond, which defines a covalent bond as the sharing of an electron pair, works through why carbon can neither gain nor lose four electrons, and ties the low melting points and poor conductivity to the absence of ions.

context: Draw the electron dot structures for
solution:
**Ethanoic acid, \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\).**

Bonds to draw as shared pairs:

- **\(\text{C}_1\)** — three shared pairs with three hydrogen atoms, and one with \(\text{C}_2\).
- **\(\text{C}_2\)** — a **double bond** (two shared pairs) to one oxygen, and a single bond to the oxygen of the \(-\text{OH}\) group.
- That second **oxygen** — one shared pair with \(\text{C}_2\), one with the hydrogen, plus two lone pairs.
- The **double-bonded oxygen** carries two lone pairs of its own.

Check: both carbons have 8 electrons around them, both oxygens have 8, and all four hydrogens have 2.
groundedIn: §4.1 Bonding in Carbon — the Covalent Bond, which builds the electron dot structures of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen and methane (Figs. 4.1 to 4.5) by counting valence electrons and completing each atom's octet, with Table 4.4 for the functional groups named here.

context: Draw the electron dot structures for
solution:
**Hydrogen sulphide, \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\).**

Sulphur has **six** valence electrons and needs two more; each hydrogen has one and needs one more.

- **One shared pair** between sulphur and each hydrogen — two single bonds.
- Sulphur keeps **two lone pairs**.

Drawn as \(\text{H} - \text{S} - \text{H}\). Sulphur then counts 8 electrons (4 in its lone pairs plus 4 shared in) and each hydrogen counts 2.
groundedIn: §4.1 Bonding in Carbon — the Covalent Bond, which builds the electron dot structures of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen and methane (Figs. 4.1 to 4.5) by counting valence electrons and completing each atom's octet, with Table 4.4 for the functional groups named here.

context: Draw the electron dot structures for
solution:
**Propanone, \(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CO} - \text{CH}_3\).**

- **\(\text{C}_1\)** and **\(\text{C}_3\)** — each shares one pair with each of three hydrogen atoms and one pair with the middle carbon.
- **\(\text{C}_2\)**, the middle carbon — one shared pair with each of its two carbon neighbours, and a **double bond** (two shared pairs) to the oxygen.
- The **oxygen** carries two lone pairs alongside its double bond.

The carbonyl group sits on the **middle** carbon, which is what makes propanone a ketone rather than an aldehyde. Every carbon counts 8 electrons, the oxygen counts 8, each hydrogen 2.
groundedIn: §4.1 Bonding in Carbon — the Covalent Bond, which builds the electron dot structures of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen and methane (Figs. 4.1 to 4.5) by counting valence electrons and completing each atom's octet, with Table 4.4 for the functional groups named here.

context: Draw the electron dot structures for
solution:
**Fluorine, \(\text{F}_2\).**

Each fluorine atom has **seven** valence electrons and needs just one more, so the two atoms share **one pair** between them — a single covalent bond.

- **One shared pair** between the two atoms: \(\text{F} - \text{F}\).
- **Three lone pairs** left on each atom.

Each fluorine then counts 8 electrons (6 in its lone pairs plus 2 shared in), completing both octets. This is the same pattern as the chlorine molecule.
groundedIn: §4.1 Bonding in Carbon — the Covalent Bond, which builds the electron dot structures of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen and methane (Figs. 4.1 to 4.5) by counting valence electrons and completing each atom's octet, with Table 4.4 for the functional groups named here.

stem: What is an homologous series? Explain with an example.
solution:
**A homologous series is a family of carbon compounds in which the same functional group is attached to carbon chains of different lengths.**

Its members share these features:

- The **same functional group**, so they have very similar **chemical** properties.
- Successive members differ by a **\(-\text{CH}_2-\) unit**, that is, by \(\text{CH}_2\) in formula.
- **Physical** properties such as melting and boiling point change **gradually** along the series as the chain gets longer.
- All members fit one **general formula**.

**Example — the alkanes**, general formula \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}\):

\(\text{CH}_4\) (methane), \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\) (ethane), \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\) (propane), \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\) (butane)

Each differs from the one before it by exactly \(\text{CH}_2\). The alcohols (\(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\), \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\), …), all carrying the \(-\text{OH}\) group, are another such series.
groundedIn: §4.2.4 Homologous Series, which defines the series as the same functional group attached to carbon chains of different lengths and tabulates the successive difference of \(\text{CH}_2\) (Table 4.3).

stem: How can ethanol and ethanoic acid be differentiated on the basis of their physical and chemical properties?
solution:
| Basis | Ethanol \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) | Ethanoic acid \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\) |
|---|---|---|
| **Smell** | Pleasant smell | Sharp smell of vinegar |
| **Melting point** | 156 K — stays liquid in winter | 290 K — often **freezes** in cold climates, hence *glacial* acetic acid |
| **Litmus** | Neutral; no change | Turns **blue litmus red** |
| **With sodium hydrogencarbonate** | No reaction | **Brisk effervescence** of \(\text{CO}_2\), which turns lime water milky |
| **With a base such as NaOH** | No reaction | Neutralised to a salt and water |

**The decisive chemical test** is the hydrogencarbonate one, because the gas is visible and can itself be confirmed:

\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\)

The **freezing point** is the decisive physical one — pure ethanoic acid solidifies on a cold day while ethanol does not come close.
groundedIn: §4.4.1 Properties of Ethanol and §4.4.2 Properties of Ethanoic Acid, with Table 4.1 for the melting points, Activity 4.7 for the litmus and pH comparison and Activity 4.9 for the reaction with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates.

stem: Why does micelle formation take place when soap is added to water? Will a micelle be formed in other solvents such as ethanol also?
solution:
**Why micelles form in water.** A soap molecule has **two ends with different properties**: an ionic head that is **hydrophilic** (it interacts with water) and a long hydrocarbon tail that is **hydrophobic** (it interacts with hydrocarbons, not water).

Dropped into water, the molecule cannot satisfy both ends at once. The tails escape the water by clustering together, and the ionic heads face outwards into it — giving a sphere with **the hydrocarbon tails in the interior and the ionic ends on the surface**. That cluster is a **micelle**. Oily dirt collects in the middle, and the micelles stay suspended as a colloid because the like charges on their surfaces repel each other.

**Will a micelle form in ethanol? No.** Ethanol is not water: the hydrocarbon tail is perfectly **soluble in it**, so there is nothing for the tail to escape from. With both ends comfortable in the solvent, the molecules have no reason to cluster, they simply dissolve, and no micelle forms.
groundedIn: §4.5 Soaps and Detergents with Fig. 4.12 and the micelle note — soaps are molecules whose two ends have differing properties, one hydrophilic and one hydrophobic, and the cluster with hydrophobic tails in the interior and ionic ends on the surface is called a micelle.

stem: Why are carbon and its compounds used as fuels for most applications?
solution:
Because burning them **releases a large amount of heat**, and does so conveniently.

- Carbon in **all** its allotropic forms burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide **along with the release of heat and light**, and most carbon compounds release a large amount of heat and light on burning too.
- With enough air the combustion is **complete**, giving a clean blue flame and only carbon dioxide and water — no solid residue to clear away.
- They are **easy to store and transport**, and come as solids (coal), liquids (petroleum) and gases (LPG), so there is a form to suit almost any application.

Carbon and its compounds are consequently some of our major sources of fuel.
groundedIn: §4.3.1 Combustion, which states that carbon in all its allotropic forms burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide with the release of heat and light, and the chapter summary, which names carbon and its compounds as major sources of fuels.

stem: Explain the formation of scum when hard water is treated with soap.
solution:
**Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts**, and soap is the **sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid**.

When the two meet, the calcium and magnesium ions **displace the sodium or potassium** in the soap, giving the calcium and magnesium salts of the same carboxylic acid. Those salts are **insoluble in water**, so they separate out as a white, curdy solid — the **scum**.

Two consequences follow, and both are familiar:

- Soap used up in forming scum is no longer available for cleaning, so **a much larger amount of soap is needed**.
- Foam forms only with difficulty, and the insoluble scum is left behind on the cloth or the skin after washing.

This is the problem **detergents** solve: their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, so they stay effective in hard water.
groundedIn: §4.5 Soaps and Detergents with Activity 4.11 — the white curdy precipitate in hard water — and the closing paragraph, which attributes scum to the reaction of soap with the calcium and magnesium salts that cause hardness.

stem: What change will you observe if you test soap with litmus paper (red and blue)?
solution:
**Red litmus turns blue; blue litmus stays blue.** Soap is **basic** in nature.

The reason is in how soap is made. A soap is the **sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid** — the salt of a **strong base** (sodium or potassium hydroxide) and a **weak acid** (the carboxylic acid). A salt of that combination is basic, with a pH above 7.

So the only visible change is on the **red** strip.
groundedIn: §4.4.2 Properties of Ethanoic Acid, which states that carboxylic acids are weak acids and that saponification with the alkali sodium hydroxide gives the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid, and §4.5, which defines soaps as sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.

stem: What is hydrogenation? What is its industrial application?
solution:
**Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated hydrocarbon in the presence of a catalyst such as palladium or nickel, converting it into a saturated hydrocarbon.** It is an **addition reaction**.

\(\text{Unsaturated hydrocarbon} + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Ni}} \text{Saturated hydrocarbon}\)

A **catalyst** is a substance that causes a reaction to occur or to proceed at a different rate without itself being affected by the reaction.

**Industrial application — hardening of vegetable oils.** Vegetable oils have long **unsaturated** carbon chains and are liquid; animal fats have **saturated** chains and are solid. Hydrogenating a vegetable oil over a **nickel catalyst** saturates those chains and turns the oil into a solid fat, which is how vanaspati ghee is made.

Worth noting from the same section: oils containing unsaturated fatty acids are the healthier choice for cooking, so hydrogenation improves keeping quality at a cost.
groundedIn: §4.3.3 Addition Reaction, which defines the reaction, names palladium and nickel as catalysts, defines a catalyst, and gives the hydrogenation of vegetable oils using a nickel catalyst as the common industrial use.

stem: Which of the following hydrocarbons undergo addition reactions: C₂H₆, C₃H₈, C₃H₆, C₂H₂ and CH₄.
solution:
**Only the unsaturated ones: \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\) and \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\).**

An addition reaction needs a **double or triple bond** for the hydrogen to add across. Test each formula against the alkane general formula \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}\) — a compound that matches it is saturated:

| Compound | \(2n+2\) | Hydrogens | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\text{CH}_4\) | 4 | 4 | Saturated — no addition |
| \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\) | 6 | 6 | Saturated — no addition |
| \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\) | 8 | 8 | Saturated — no addition |
| \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\) | 8 | 6 | **Unsaturated** — one double bond |
| \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\) | 6 | 2 | **Unsaturated** — one triple bond |

The three saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive and undergo **substitution** reactions instead, with chlorine in sunlight.
groundedIn: §4.3.3 Addition Reaction (unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen over a catalyst) and §4.3.4 Substitution Reaction (saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive and are substituted instead), with §4.2.1 for the saturated/unsaturated distinction.

stem: Give a test that can be used to differentiate between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.
solution:
**The burning test.** Burn a sample of each in air and watch the flame.

- A **saturated** hydrocarbon burns with a **clean blue flame**.
- An **unsaturated** hydrocarbon burns with a **yellow, sooty flame** with a great deal of black smoke, leaving a sooty deposit on a metal plate held above it.

One caution, which the book itself gives: **limiting the supply of air makes even a saturated hydrocarbon burn with a sooty flame**, so the test is trustworthy only when air is plentiful.

**A cleaner laboratory test** is the reaction with bromine water. An unsaturated hydrocarbon **decolourises bromine water**, because the bromine adds across the double or triple bond; a saturated hydrocarbon leaves the colour unchanged, having no such bond to add across.
groundedIn: §4.3.1 Combustion with Activities 4.3 and 4.4 — saturated hydrocarbons give a clean flame while unsaturated ones give a yellow sooty flame, and limiting the air supply causes even saturated ones to smoke — with §4.3.3 for addition across an unsaturated bond.

stem: Explain the mechanism of the cleaning action of soaps.
solution:
Most dirt is **oily**, and oil does not dissolve in water — which is why water alone will not clean cloth. Soap works because its molecule can hold on to both.

**1. Two ends, two affinities.** A soap molecule is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid. Its **ionic end is hydrophilic** and interacts with water; its **long hydrocarbon tail is hydrophobic** and interacts with oil.

**2. The micelle forms.** Soap molecules surround a droplet of oily dirt with their **tails buried in the oil and their ionic ends facing outwards** into the water. This cluster is a **micelle**, and it traps the dirt at its centre.

**3. An emulsion is made.** The micelles keep the oil suspended in the water as an emulsion. They do not clump together and settle, because their like-charged surfaces **repel one another**.

**4. Agitation and rinsing.** Beating or scrubbing loosens the dirt from the fibres so the micelles can carry it off, and rinsing washes the suspended micelles — dirt and all — away with the water.

The micelles are large enough to scatter light, which is why a soap solution looks cloudy.
groundedIn: §4.5 Soaps and Detergents with Activity 4.10, Fig. 4.12 and Fig. 4.13, and the micelle note — the ionic end interacting with water, the carbon chain with oil, the emulsion, the ion-ion repulsion that keeps micelles in colloidal solution and the light scattering that makes the solution cloudy.
